name: Niger
summary: Niger publishes no official procedure for bringing a coffin into the country. Expect to obtain an authorisation from the Niger embassy or consulate in the country of death and to send the body embalmed in a hermetically sealed coffin; confirm everything with the mission first.
documents: Death certificate (French or with French translation; confirm with the Niger mission)
Certificate of non-contagious disease
Embalming certificate
Coffin sealing record
Exit or transport permit from the country of death
Passport or ID of the deceased
Authorisation or visa from the Niger embassy or consulate (not officially documented online)
coffin: No official Nigerien specification found. Plan for the international standard of a hermetically sealed zinc-lined inner coffin in a wooden outer coffin, and confirm with the Niger mission.
embalming: No official rule published; embalming is normally expected for a long-haul air transfer. Confirm with the Niger mission.
consular: Niger has no published repatriation procedure. Contact the Niger embassy or consulate in the country of death before booking; documents may need legalisation rather than an apostille. Niger is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement, so no mortuary laissez-passer replaces the consular step. The French embassy in Niamey is closed until further notice and cannot provide consular help.
arrival: No official information on health or customs clearance at Niamey Diori Hamani airport was found. Arrange a local receiving funeral home or family member in advance.
private_aviation: UK travel advice reports gunfire near Niamey's Diori Hamani International Airport in 2026 and warns that commercial flights can be disrupted at short notice. A private flight needs landing permission and must use an international airport with customs and health control.
private_jet_note: Security incidents near Niamey airport in 2026; check airport status and landing permits before departure.
export: No official procedure for taking a body out of Niger was found. Expect a death certificate, a medical certificate, embalming and a sealed coffin, plus the authorisations of the local authorities and of the destination country's consulate; confirm with a local funeral home.
export_points: No official export procedure published
French embassy in Niamey closed; French families need other channels
Destination country's consulate approval usually needed
Check airport and security situation before planning

name: Nigeria
summary: A coffin can enter Nigeria only with a waiver from the Federal Ministry of Health (Port Health Services, Abuja) followed by a letter for shipment of human remains from the Nigerian mission in the country of death. The body must be embalmed and placed in a hermetically sealed metal casket.
documents: Port Health waiver from the Federal Ministry of Health, Abuja (request letter to the Minister of Health giving date, place and cause of death and age)
Death certificate (notarised or certified copy) and medical certificate of death
Burial transit permit or certificate for shipping the body out of the country of death
Non-communicable disease letter or certificate from a coroner, medical examiner or health agency
Notarised embalmer's affidavit or embalming certificate
Notarised funeral home letter confirming a hermetically sealed metal casket containing only the remains
Medical examiner's report if applicable
Deceased's Nigerian passport, or a notarised affidavit from a relative holding a Nigerian passport
Funeral home request letter to the mission and contact details of the receiving party in Nigeria
Mission fee and prepaid return envelope
coffin: A hermetically sealed metal casket is required, confirmed by a notarised funeral home letter stating that it contains only the remains of the deceased.
embalming: Embalming is required, evidenced by a notarised embalmer's affidavit or embalming certificate.
consular: After the Federal Ministry of Health waiver is granted, the Nigerian embassy, high commission or consulate checks the file and issues a letter (permission) for shipment of human remains. Fees vary by mission: 50 USD in Atlanta; 50 CAD per page plus a 50 CAD administrative fee in Ottawa, plus a 5,000 naira international waiver fee payable to Port Health Services. Ottawa quotes 10 business days.
arrival: Port Health Services check the waiver and documents at the arrival airport before customs release to the family or funeral home. Arrival-side formalities are not detailed on the mission pages consulted.
private_aviation: The Port Health waiver and mission letter are required whatever the aircraft. A private or charter flight should land at an international airport with Port Health presence (for example Lagos or Abuja) with the waiver, mission letter and original documents travelling with the casket.
private_jet_note: Do not take off before the Federal Ministry of Health waiver and the mission letter are in hand.
export: UK government guidance for taking a body out of Nigeria lists the death certificate, a death certificate from the National Population Commission, permission to remove the body issued by a coroner, the passport of the deceased and an infection-free declaration from the Ministry of Health; rules vary by location. The body must be embalmed (usually after any post-mortem) and placed in a metal casket. Cremation of a foreign national is possible.
export_points: National Population Commission death certificate
Coroner's permission to remove the body
Ministry of Health infection-free declaration
Embalming and a metal casket are required

name: Rwanda
summary: To bring a body into Rwanda, the family or funeral home applies to the Rwandan embassy or high commission in the country of death for a body repatriation document (burial permit), with the death certificate, a non-communicable disease certificate and an embalming certificate.
documents: Request letter to the Ambassador or High Commission (from next of kin or funeral home) with contact details of a relative in Rwanda
Death certificate
Certificate of non-communicable disease
Certificate of embalming (mortuary preparation report)
Certificate or permit for shipping the body out of the country of death (requested by the Ottawa mission)
Copies of the deceased's identity documents
Mission form and fee where applicable (Ottawa: burial permit form, free; Washington: 30 USD; Doha: 40 QR)
coffin: The Rwandan mission pages do not specify casket requirements. Follow the airline and IATA standard (hermetically sealed inner container in a wooden outer coffin) and confirm with the mission.
embalming: Embalming is required: every Rwandan mission page consulted lists a certificate of embalming.
consular: The Rwandan embassy or high commission in the country of death issues the body repatriation document or burial permit. The Ottawa mission processes it free of charge in up to 3 business days; Washington charges 30 USD and Doha 40 QR. Incomplete applications are returned.
arrival: No official description of arrival clearance at Kigali was found. Carry the mission document and originals with the coffin; a relative or funeral home in Rwanda collects it.
private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights was found. Land at an international airport with customs and health control (Kigali International) with the mission document travelling with the coffin.
private_jet_note: Have the mission's repatriation document issued before departure and carry the originals on board.
export: For a body leaving Rwanda, UK guidance says a local death certificate, a certificate of embalming and a certificate giving permission to transfer the body are always required. Local formalities normally take three or four days for a natural death; police investigation of sudden or suspicious deaths can delay release. The only crematorium is the Hindu Mandal crematorium in Bugesera, which needs district authority permission.

Permission to transfer the body

embalming: No official entry rule published; Senegal itself requires a certificate of embalming for bodies leaving the country, and embalming is normally expected for air transport. Ask the consulate about religious washing before sealing.

name: South Africa
summary: A coffin can enter South Africa only with an import permit issued in advance by the National Department of Health (Director-General of Health); no permit is issued at the point of entry. The body must be embalmed (unless religion forbids it) and sealed in an airtight container inside a sturdy non-transparent coffin.
documents: Import permit from the National Department of Health, applied for by email to humanremainspermits@health.gov.za (valid 30 days)
Cover letter from the embassy or funeral undertaker naming the deceased, place of burial, date, place and cause of death, the South African point of entry and the type of transport
Death certificate clearly stating the cause of death (certified English translation if needed)
ID document or passport of the deceased
Embalming certificate (or statement of the alternative preservation method if embalming is refused for religious reasons)
Letter from a family member requesting the import, with their ID or passport and contact details
Non-infectious (or infectious) disease certificate signed by a registered medical practitioner or forensic pathologist
Certificate of Competence of the South African funeral undertaker who will receive the remains
coffin: For non-infectious remains, the body is sealed in an airtight container and placed in a sturdy, non-transparent coffin. Infectious remains must also be placed in a polythene bag. The sealed container may not be opened without approval of a health officer.
embalming: Embalming is required and certified. If embalming cannot be done for religious reasons, a statement from the relevant authority describing the alternative preservation method must be supplied. Bodies of persons who died of smallpox, anthrax or viral haemorrhagic fever must not be embalmed.
consular: A South African embassy or the funeral undertaker can submit the permit application; the Consulate General in New York, for example, sends a request letter with the deceased's particulars to Pretoria. Documents not in English need a certified translation. South Africa is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: Port Health (Border Management Authority) detains and inspects human remains on arrival and grants clearance only once permit conditions are met. Remains arriving without a permit can be held in a mortuary at the importer's cost and, if no permit follows within 30 days, buried by order of the Director-General. A certified local undertaker receives the coffin.
private_aviation: The permit application must name the point of entry and the type of transport, so a private flight must land at the declared port of entry with Port Health (Border Management Authority) presence. The regulations require an airtight container in a sealed coffin on public transport and an approved coffin or container otherwise; confirm acceptable containers with the Department of Health.
private_jet_note: The Department of Health permit must be issued before take-off and must name your arrival airport.
export: Leaving South Africa also requires an export permit from the National Department of Health (applied for by email; about 2 working days once complete). The file includes a cover letter naming the exit point and transport, death certificate with cause of death, ID or passport (or a police affidavit), an embalming certificate stamped by the undertaker and embalmer with the address of the embalming premises, a family request letter, a non-infectious disease certificate, the Notice of Death form (BI-1663), the Burial Order from the Department of Home Affairs and the undertaker's Certificate of Competence.
export_points: Department of Health export permit, about 2 working days
Burial Order from Home Affairs and BI-1663 notice of death
Embalming and airtight container in a sealed coffin
Port Health inspection at departure
